abstract: Dosage compensation (DC) restores the expression balance between the X chromosome and autosomes in males. How this chromosome-wide regulation is precisely regulated to accommodate the heterogeneous functions and dosage-sensitivity among X-linked genes is unclear. To address this, we analyse the epigenomic and 3D genome data of mostly sexed samples from embryos to adults of Drosophila melanogaster, whose DC is known to be mediated by three classes of X-enriched sequence elements of HAS/CES, PionX and 1.6883F satellites. We find that about 30% of the X-linked genes are compensated specifically in one or a few male stages or tissues, indicated by their significant bindings of the DC-associated protein or H4K16ac histone modification. These specifically (SDC) or facultatively (FDC) compensated genes are more likely to have a developmentally regulated expression and a highly relevant function with the stage or tissue where they are compensated. They show a higher level of co-binding of facultative heterochromatin hallmark H3K27me3 than the constitutively (CDC) compensated housekeeping genes. CDC genes preferentially harbor constitutive long-range (>1Mb) contacts (LRCs) with other CDC genes and the HAS elements, which form by the onset of DC in embryos. While SDC and FDC genes show developmentally increased LRCs with the respective type of genes and the PionX elements and 1.6883F satellites. The CDC genes and their interacting partners more often coincide with the constitutive boundaries of topologically associated domains, while the other DC genes tend to coincide with the developmentally regulated boundaries. Our results uncover that the Drosophila DC is regulated through separate chromatin modules between housekeeping vs. developmental genes involving different combinations of regulatory sequence elements and 3D genome contacts. This provides broad implications for the hierarchical regulation of DC against different developmental and gene backgrounds among other organisms.
